earlier_scan.source_named: Middleton, John. 2023. Preverbal Determiners and the Passive in Moriori. Oceanic Linguistics 62(1):117-142 (paywalled); also Clark, Ross. 1994. Moriori and Maori: the linguistic evidence.

sources.citation: Williams, H. W. 1919. Some notes on the language of the Chatham Islands. Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute 51:415-422 (Art. XXXVI)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Vowel and consonant correspondences with Maori, vowel dropping with compensatory lengthening, aspirated/palatalised H K T. On quantity p. 418: 'In a number of words a vowel has become long where in Maori we have a short vowel.. It is possible that in reciting the legends a rhythmical diction may have been adopted which placed on certain vowels a stress which did not accord with that of the normal pronunciation.' No statement of where word stress falls.
Orthography table and remarks on aspirated/palatalised k h t and 'consistent suppression of terminal vowels'; nothing on stress. Cites Taiuru 2016, Richards 2018, Shand 1911.

sources.citation: Hokotehi Moriori Trust. 2024-2026. Ta rē Moriori revival teaching materials / Moriori Language Week resources (moriori.co.nz; 'Resources coming soon')
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Revival materials typically include a pronunciation guide that states a stress convention (likely Maori-style); would be a secondary, prescriptive statement only.

sources.citation: Middleton, John. 2024. A Moriori tale: Ko Tahopuni rauu Ko Paonga. Waka Kuaka / The Journal of the Polynesian Society 133(2):217-238. DOI 10.15286/jps.133.2.217-238
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Short phonology/orthography note p. 219: 5 vowels /i e a o u/, 10 consonants /p t k f h m n ŋ r w/ (Clark 2000); a palatal affricate <tch>/<tc> unique among East Polynesian, possibly non-phonemic; 'Vowels can be long (with a macron or double letters) or short'; word-final vowels often clipped (Shand 1911:1), written with apostrophe; breves on final vowels = 'scarcely or not heard'. Nothing on stress or accent placement.

sources.citation: Middleton, John. 2023. Preverbal Determiners and the Passive in Moriori. Oceanic Linguistics 62(1):117-142. DOI 10.1353/ol.2023.0003
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Full text (pp. 117-139 + refs) captured via Internet Archive copy of the Project MUSE page; no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent', 'prosod', 'syllable'. Only phonological remarks: breves in Shand's texts 'are assumed to be macrons' (p. 118) and phonologically conditioned allomorphy of determiners (ta/tch/tV, p. 121-122, citing Clark 2000). Silent on stress placement.

sources.citation: Richards, Rhys. 2018. Comparisons of Moriori, Maori, and Easter Island cognates. Rapa Nui Journal 31(1):38-40. DOI 10.1353/rnj.0.0001
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Cognate percentages only; 'Apart from differences in pronunciation, which were considerable, a Moriori speaker would have understood a Maori speaker well'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Taiuru, Karaitiana N. 2016. Word list and analysis of te reo Moriori. Self-published (ISBN 978-0-9582597-0-5), CC BY-NC
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Analysis' section (pp. 4-7) is a lightly edited reproduction of Williams 1919 (vowel/consonant changes, aspirated H K T 'stressed pronunciation' = the aspirated/palatalised consonants, not accent); then a compiled wordlist. No stress placement statement. Not a linguist's work (author's own disclaimer).

sources.citation: Skinner, H. D. 1923. The Morioris of Chatham Islands. Memoirs of the Bernice P. Bishop Museum 9(1)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 'Language' p. 43 only quotes Williams 1919 and speculates on affinity with Kai-Tahu Maori (hoko- causative, k for ng). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Shand, Alexander. 1911. The Moriori People of the Chatham Islands: their history and traditions. Memoirs of the Polynesian Society 2. Wellington. (reprint of JPS vols 3-7, 1894-1898)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Introduction note p. 1: 'little attempt has been made to give the peculiar pronunciation of the Moriori people.. It frequently happens that the last letter in a word (always a vowel) is hardly pronounced at all, thus making it appear that the word ends in a consonant.' Note 11 (p. ~91): 'The i is scarcely heard; it is not clear and separate as in Maori pronunciation.' Nothing on accent/stress (the 3 hits for 'stress' are non-linguistic).

sources.citation: Deighton, Samuel. 1889. A Moriori vocabulary (letter from S. Deighton, Esq., R.M., Chatham Islands, forwarding the first portion of). Appendix to the Journals of the House of Representatives 1889 Session I, G-5, pp. 1-7
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Covering letter (6 Sept 1887), p. 1: 't' pronounced 'teh' (tamaiti > tchimitchi), 'the final i being hardly sounded: in fact, in the greater proportion of the words the final vowel is almost dropped, or rather clipped off'; 'a more guttural pronunciation than is shown in the Maori language'. English-Moriori-Maori wordlist follows. Nothing on stress/accent.

sources.citation: Dieffenbach, Ernest. 1841. An account of the Chatham Islands. Journal of the Royal Geographical Society of London 11:195-215
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp. 209-210: Moriori is 'merely a dialect of that of New Zealand.. differing less in words and construction than in pronunciation.. The same words are differently accented; the last syllables of a word are often drawled out; o is used for a, e for ai, &c.' Examples: Wai > We, A'rero > O'rero, Moe > Mo, Motu > Wutu. Impressionistic; no rule of stress placement.
